items.title: Adoration of Child (Tondo: Holy Family and Baptist)
items.description:
An oil and wood painting depicting the Holy Family and John the Baptist. The Virgin Mary, Saint Joseph, and John sit around baby Jesus and gaze down at him. Jesus stares outward at the viewer, meeting our gaze.
The Virgin Mary is centered in the composition, wearing her blue and green mantle and a red tunic. Her head is partially covered in a wrap. A halo is faintly seen above her head. She is on her knees, leaning over baby Jesus, her hands in prayer.
In the middleground, to the viewer's right, sits Saint Joseph. His beard is clean and neatly trimmed into two points. He, like Mary, is dressed in a red tunic. A light brown mantle is laid over his lap. A faint halo is seen above his head. He rests his chin in his hands as he looks towards the baby Jesus.
To the right of Mary (the viewer's left), a baby John the Baptist leans over Jesus. He is dressed in a more muted blue than Mary; his mantle is held closed by a red strip of fabric tied around his waist. Visible over his head of curly hair is a halo.
Between John and Mary, laying on the floor, is baby Jesus. He lays on a dark blue pillow or mat. A shawl, nearly transparent, is draped over his waist and around his shoulder. He clutches the end in his right fist. A halo is seen above his head.

On the table is inscribed: "LA PIV' GRAN VITORIA/ CHE POSSA HAVERE/ VN HVOMO E'VINCERE/ SE' STESSO." This is a passage from Plato's "Laws."

items.title: Painted Wood Shutter (India)
items.description:
An oil painting on a wooden shutter. The window frame (boarder) is painted yellow with a repeating four leaf motif and blue and white flowers. Down the center, a wooden beam is painted the same yellow, this time with a repeating white flower and yellow flower pattern.
The shutters depict the book of Yuddha Kanda (sometimes referred to as Landa Kanda), a story within the Sanskrit epic, "Ramayana." This part of the text is about the war between brothers Rama and Lakshmana, and Ravana. The brothers are depicted in the top left panel (Rama is blue-skinned and Lakshmana is tan-skinned), while Ravana is in the top right (he is depicted with multiple faces). Underneath them, on the bottom half of the panels, their respective armies are depicted.

items.title: Vue de Villefranche sur Mer
items.description:
A painting of a seaside done on the canvas of a tambourine. The image is done in oil paints and the seaside town is visible at the left of the image in the mid-ground. A group of three sailors is docking a boat - visible immediately in front of the town. They seem to be pulling up to a bank, where yellow and red-brown sand is visible, rather than a dock. The right half of the image shows the sea, stretching out in an inlet with more of the town visible on a far bank through fog or haze.
Title translates to "View of Villefranche-sur-Mer." Villefranche-Sur-Mer is a small town in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region on the French Riviera. The village name would translate to Villefranch on sea (or on the sea).

items.title: Christ Removing Merchants from the Temple
items.description:
Oil Painting on Canvas. Christ, dressed in a red robe and blue cloak, stands prominent as the central figure of the painting. His right arm is raised as his left gestures in a point, expelling the Merchants from the Temple. All around him, the merchants cower from him near the borders of the painting. The background is comprised mostly of a large column and wall of the temple itself, although a landscape extends on the left side of the painting. Suggestions of normal life - or at least life as normal before Christ begins his expulsion - are scattered throughout the painting, including the baskets, a chest full of coins and many animals.
The artist is unknown but the skill in rendering the figures and the daily realism of the details reveals a highly skilled artist of Bolognese origin.

items.title: The Dream of St. Jerome
items.description:
Oil Painting on Canvas. Depicts Saint Jerome, clutching a cross in the lower right quadrant of the painting. His looks upward, toward where the Virgin Mary is depicted in heaven, attended to by a croup of cherubs. A lone cherub stands with a lion at the lower left side behind the saint. The lion is meant to be his companion, who loyally followed Saint Jerome after he removed a thorn from it's paw.
Saint Jerome was a very important early Christian Scholar during his life. His translation of the Bible into Latin was the standard edition used throughout the Middle Ages, and his influence on monasticism would last for several centuries after his death. It is said that in the spring of 375, Saint Jerome dreamed that he was hauled before a heavenly court and was accused of being a follower of the Roman Philosopher Cicero, rather than a follower of Christ. He was whipped for the crime before waking. After the dream he vowed never to read or own pagan literature again.
The painting can be placed in the Venetian area of the second half of the 18th century, in the circle of G. Diziani.

items.title: Madonna and Child with Saint John, et al.
items.description:
Oil Painting on Panel. The Madonna sits at the center of the painting with the infant Christ on her lap. To their left (when viewing), a young Saint John (identified throughout the paperwork in Italian as San Giovannino) holds his Cross in his right hand with his arms crossed over his chest in adoration.
Two people stand with the trio, a man on the left side, and a woman on the right. They are identified as Saint Zachariah, the father of John the Baptist, and either Saint Elisabetta or Anna in documentation. As the female saint holds a book, which is an attribute of Anna (Saint Anne in English), this is her more likely identity. Saint Anne is the mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus Christ.
The Iconography in this image is interesting,as the depiction of a sleeping infant Christ on the Virgin Mary's lap is usually reserved for images of the two of them alone, rather than images of them with other people.
A crack runs through the center of the image, thankfully bypassing the important details of each of the figures. Restoration work has been done periodically on the image.

items.title: The Last Supper
items.description:
A Travel Icon from the Cretan School. The image depicts the 12 Apostles, all dressed in blue and red, sat in a helical layout. Christ is present in the image, represented by the symbol "I H S" monogram (shown within the motif of a shining sun) at the lower center of the image. This monogram, along with the sunburst which surrounds it is rendered using the pastiglia technique, so it stands three dimensional above the rest of the scene, which is painted directly onto the flat panel.
The background is a geometric interior, which recedes behind the images of the Apostles. At the top of the panel, the architecture of a decorated arch, along with corner decorations are suggested through the same pastiglia technique as the Monogram of Christ.
The parts of this painting rendered using the pastiglia technique have been all been gilt or painted over in gold.

The center panel shows the Descent of Christ to earth following the Resurrection. Within the same panel two additional scenes, one of Christ judgment the souls of men, and one of what might be Christ overseeing a baptism At the top, three haloed angels sit within the arch.
The right panel (when viewing) shows Saint Catherine, dressed in red with gold accents and a blue cloak. A crown sits on her head and she is haloed. Above her, in the arch, stands the Virgin Mary.
The left panel (when viewing) shows Saint Pacôme (Probably in English: Pachomius the Great), dressed in gold and blue. He wears a cap, a long beard and is haloed. Above him, in the arch, stands the Angel Gabriel.

items.description:

items.title: Crucifixion
items.description:
A large wooden Icon Panel, painted to depict the Crucifixion. The center of the image is dominated by an inlaid metal cross, (likely brass?). The cross has been carved with a detail of Christ crucified, although the crown of thorns has been omitted in favor of showing a halo. The nails through his feet and palms are detailed. Above his head angels look down toward Christ. At his feet a small detail of city or fortress towers extends to either side and a scull is seemingly buried at his feet. The rest of the panel is painted depicting the scene of the crucifixion and what follows.
To his left stands three women. While it is not confirmed, these figures are presumably the Three Marys to witness the crucifixion (the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalen, and Mary Clopas). All three are haloed and wear blue/green dresses. The right-most of the trio looks toward the crucifixion with her hand raised to her face as if Crying. The central figure stands behind the other two, looking away from the crucifixion. Both of these women have shawls that wrap over the head which are a dark, wine-red color. The third figure, to the left side of the trio, also has the same style shawl, but it is bright rid. She also gazes toward the scene of the crucifixion.
To the right side of the inlaid cross, stand two more onlookers to the crucifixion. The first figure is a haloed woman. She is dressed in a green dress with a bright red shawl, but it is not warped, leaving her hair uncovered. Her identity is unconfirmed, but her lack of a veil suggests she may be Veronica. To the right of this female saint is a soldier, also haloed. He is dressed in armor, a red cloak with a white hood and boots. His identity is also unconfirmed, but as he carries a spear he may be interpreted as Longinus.
Above the cross in the upper left hand corner of the image The Descent from the Cross is depicted: six people work to lower Christ from the cross. On the left of the cross stand two of the women from the trio in the lower scene: The woman with the bright shawl and the crying women in dark red. To the right, the same male and female unidentified saints. At the top two new figures work to lower Christ from the cross. These new figures are also haloed, and are traditionally identified as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, though their identities are unconfirmed here.
A third scene is depicted in the upper right corner. In this scene a group of 5 prepare Christ's body for burial. Christ is laid on a golden table. The same three women (The one shawled in red, the crying woman, and the woman with her head uncovered) stand over the body while the two men who lowered him from the cross stand at the edges of the scene, holding the funeral shroud, preparing to wrap the body.
The top and bottom of the panel are painted with a scrolling motif in gold, green and red paint. The left and right borders depict haloed saints, three to each side. It is possible that these six figures may overlap with the onlookers portrayed within the scenes of the main panel, but their identifications are not able to be read.

items.title: Mother of God Galaktotrophousa
items.description:
Known in English as either an Icon of The Virgin as "the Milk-Giver" or The Virgin Nursing. The image is a painted wooden Icon panel that depicts an infant Christ held in the arms of the Virgin as he drinks from her breast.
The Virgin is depicted wearing a blue dress with a red hooded cloak - a transparent white veil can also be seen underneath the hood. She supports the infant Christ, holding him up to right side. Her head is tilted toward him, but her gaze is directed to the viewer. Christ himself is dressed in white and gold. He sits upright in his mother's arms, with both hands grasping her breast to drink. His Gaze is directed up toward his mother.
The motif of the nursing Madonna was found in early Christian Mythology, and is an evocative representation of the human nature of the son of God. References to he theme can be found in Byzantine homilies and hymns with comparisons drawn between the milk from Mary's breast and the blood from Jesus' side. The comparison links the two theologically and creates a connection between the Mother of God Galaktotrophousa and Christ's suffering on the cross.
The background of this painting is golden, but a halo is implied around the duo by a pattern punched into the surface. In order to produce this motif, the punch would be placed perpendicular to the gold surface, then struck to produce a slight indent in the gesso beneath. This had to be done when the gesso was still soft to prevent damaging the gold leaf which constitutes the top layer.

items.title: Christ Pantocrator Enthroned
items.description:
Large wooden Icon Panel, painted to depict Christ Pantocrator Enthroned. In the image, Christ sits enthroned, with his feet resting on a footstool. Dressed in an ocher yellow robe he looks toward the viewer with his right hand raised in a blessing, typical of the Pantocrator image. In his left hand he balances a gospel open on his knee. The book shows Matthew 11, 28: Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden and I will give you rest. (The writing is in Slavic and has bene translated, courtesy of Authenticator Dr. S.G. Morskin).
Around Christ the celestial world is depicted. It is comprised of many layers that together across the image and come together to symbolize the universe: The inner red diamond shape symbolizes heavenly fire (heaven of Heavens) where God resides. This is surrounded by an oval of blue, within which a motif depicting the faces and wings of seraphim (six-winged angels) is repeated. Where these figured hover, refers to heaven, behold which a red rectangle symbolizes the earth.
At the feet of Christ Thrones are depicted. In the traditional hierarchy, these angels, (together with Seraphim an cherubim) belong to the highest order of angels. They are typically depicted as circles (filled with eyes) which perpetually revolve and are propelled by small wings.
At each corner the symbols of the four evangelists are each drawn looking toward their neighbor: The Angel for Matthew in the upper left corner, the eagle for Mark in the upper right, the lion for John in the lower left and the ox for Luke in the lower left. Each depiction holds a gospel book, though these ones are closed. (Note that the allocation of these symbols are of the Orthodox Tradition, which differs from the western one where the Eagle would represent John and the Lion would represent Mark.)
Around the borders of this image restoration has resulted in the background being stripped to reveal the gesso ground.
Byzantine inspired. Eastern Orthodox Church. Central Russia.

items.title: Mother of God Pecerskaja with Saints Boris and Gleb
items.description:
Wooden icon panel painted with the images of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Christ and two Saints standing in attendance. The two saints are identified as Boris and Gleb, (Boris, the elder is probably the one on the left). They stand on either side of the Virgin and child, dressed alike except that the one on the left is bearded and bears a red cloak. The one on the right is clean shaven and wears a white cloak.
The Virgin and child sit enthroned at the center of the image. The virgin holding the Christ child in her lap. They both face the viewer, and the Christ Child raises both of his hands in blessing, one for each of the saints at their sides.
The saints are often depicted together as they were, as a pair, the first canonized saints in Kievan Rus (modern day Russia) following the state's adoption of Christianity (canonized 1071). According to 11th century stories Boris and Gleb were the younger sons of Vladimir the Great (r. 980-1015). Both of the brothers are regarded as having been pious and were venerated following their individual assassinations and martyrdoms during the internecine wars (1015–1019).

items.title: Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine
items.description:
An oil on canvas depicting the Mystic Marraige of St. Catherine. The Marraige ceremony is a common theme in Christian art, though it should be noted that there are two Saint Catherines (St. Catherine of Alexandria and St. Catherine of Sienna), both of whom may be the Saint depicted in the ceremony. Rarely they are depicted together, but this image is typical depicting Saint Catherine, crouched with her hand presneted to an infant christ. The infant sits on the Virgin Mary's lap, placing a ring on Catherine's finger. In the background two angels observe the scene.
St. Catherine of Alexandria is the Saint depicted in the Maratti image in the LFC collection. She can be identified both by her clothes - lavish dresses of yellow, white and gold with a jeweled band in her hair - as well as by the positioning of christ - who places a ring on her finger. Both the ring and her depiction as a princess identifies this Saint as Catherine of Alexandria. (Saint Catheirne of Siena is typically depicted as a Nun in the habit of the Domincan Order with the black over-robe open in the front.)
Saint Catherine of Alexandria was born in the 3rd Century C.E. in Alexandria, Roman Egypt. According to her hagiography she was both a princess and a scholar. Around the age of 14 she converted to Christianity after having a vision of the Virgin Mary and Christ. In the visoin she wed Christ, leading to the foundation of the mystic marraige. She remained a virgin as a result of this marraige. She is credited with converting hundreds of others. At the age of 18 she was martyred, following toture at the hands of Roman Emperor Maxentius. Notably, she is also identified as one of the Saints who appeared to Joan of Arc in the 15th century.

items.title: Saints Constantine and Helena (Icon)
items.description:
Wooden icon panel painted to depict Saints Constantine and Helena. The tow stand side by side, both dressed in red robes with elaborate trims and belts. They are both crowned as well as haloed and they hold a cross upright between them. The background is painted or foiled with gold. The panel is carved so that the edge sits slightly above the ground where the figures are painted, implying both a border and a degree of separation between the Saints and the image.
Saint Constantine is also known in history as Constanine I or Constantine the Great. He stands on the left hand side of the image. A roman Emperor, Constantine converted to Christianity in 312, and in 313 oversaw proclamation of the Edict of Milan, which declared religious tolerance to all Christians within the empire. He was respected by both the medieval church as a paragon of virtue, and by contemporary secular rulers as a prototype. During his reign he also founded Constantinople on the ancient city of Byzantium (modern Istanbul) and made it the Capitol of the Eastern Roman Empire. He is venerated in most Christian denominations as a Saint.
On the Right hand statement stands Saint Helena, Constantine's mother. She converted to the faith following her son's conversion. She is venerated in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Asian Orthodox and Anglican churches, as well as commemorated in the Lutheran tradition. Her major role as a saint is as the patron of Archaeologists and new discoveries, having been given this title due to her efforts to recover Christian relics during her lifetime. Constantine gave her unlimited access to the Roman Empire's treasury to fund these relic hunting journeys and she went on several pilgrimages looking for relics with the aid of these funds. According to tradition, in approximately 326 Helena completed a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Here, she oversaw the tearing down of a temple to Venus, which was thought to be built over the tomb of Jesus. During this work she discovered the True Cross, which was then brought to Rome and is the most common attribute used to identify her in artistic renditions.

items.title: Tree of Jesse (Icon)
items.description:
Wooden Icon panel. Painted with the image of the Tree of Jesse. The tree of Jesse is a Christian motif which was very popular during the Medieval period. It's use has continued to the modern day. Depictions of the tree show the Biblical genealogy of the Jesus Christ as it descends from Jesse, the father of King David.
Inspiration for the Tree of Jesse comes from a passage in Issiah: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots" (King James Version).
The Chrismon tree and the Advent calendar are sometimes referred to by modern Christians as the Jesse Tree, though this practice does not relate to the original genealogical depiction. In Advent and Chrisom traditions see the decoration of a real tree or poster with 'Chisoms' symbols representing the stories that lead up to Christmas.

items.title: Entombment of Christ
items.description:
A circular icon painting with a carved frame, painted on panel. The image depicts Christ, who is being wrapped in a white shroud and lowered into a coffin. Nicodemus and Saint Joseph of Arimathea are the ones to lower him, one at the shoulders, the other at the feet. The Virgin Mary, dressed in a red hooded cloak and robes, stands at the center of the image. She holds Christ's hand as he is lowered. Mary Magdalen, also hooded in red, though her dress beneath is blue, knees at Christ's feet with a golden cup held in her hands.
Behind the group who interacts with the body, three more saints are fathered. Saint John stands at the Virgin's left shoulder. The other two figures are identified as spice-bearing female martyrs - the spice in question is probably Myrrh, which would have been used to anoint the body. The identities of these women is difficult to pinpoint, as many Biblical women have been identified as the ones to anoint the body in different denominations and records.
At the very back of the group of figures two angels stand at the corners. The angels depict night and day, the one the left having blue wings, and the one on the left having red. The cross stands over the group as a whole, and god is depicted in heaven above. There is no background, but the foreground is painted to depict the ground.

A wooden icon panel. It is painted to depict a procession headed into a city. Tall walls surround the buildings, which only have their rooftops visible. One of the buildings has the red, domed roof of a church. Another has a blue-tiled roof and a man dressed in red stands watching the procession from a balcony. he appears to be haloed, and is probably a second image of the haloed king who stands at the center of the procession and image.
This man, probably King David, wears a grown and a red cape over a blue robe, both of which are more ornamented than the rest of the people in the procession. He plays a psaltery (a triangular stringed instrument that may be bowed, though in this image the man plays through a method of plucking).
Aside from this central figure, the procession consists mainly of men and women playing instruments, but additional figures include a man dressed in white who leads the oxen cart, and two figures dressed in blue (likely the same man depicted twice). In one version of the man, he holds a walking stick and reaches up to place his hand upon the Ark. In the second he lies upon the ground with his eyes closed, dead. Based on this depiction, the man might be Uzzah, who is said to have touched the Ark in an attempt to steady it when the cart tilted, and was immediately struck dead by God for the error.
The Ark itself is in the oxen drawn cart. It is painted mostly golden, but is also depicted as if it is encrusted in jewels. Red orbs hover near it, each with multiple wings coming off of them. This may be meant to depict the six-winged Seraphs. At the top of the image an orb ringed in gold is depicted with three rays coming off in the direction of the Ark, showing the connection between the Ark and heaven.

items.title: The Three Kings Offering Presents to the Newborn Christ
items.description:
Wooden icon panel, painted to depict the scene of the three kings going to visit the new born Christ. The kings are shown in the lower right hand corner of the painting, all three are crowned and they ride on a black, brown and white stallion respectively. The first king raises his hand to indicate the direction of the Christ child.
Beside them, St. Joseph kneels beside a river, tending to the animals from the manger where the Christ child was born. A young man plays a horn nearby. Angels fly amongst the scene, descending from heaven, depicted as an arch carved into the top of the image, where further angels sit among the clouds. Rays of golden light connect the clouded scene to the head of Christ.
At the upper left corner, the baby Jesus lays swaddled and covered by the roof of the manger. An ox lays it's head upon the boy, regarding him, and the Virgin kneels praying over the child. The Holy family are all haloed, as are the angels, though their haloes are significantly smaller. The kings and the boy are not haloed.

items.title: Three Kings Visiting the Newborn Christ
items.description:
Wooden Icon panel, depicting the Three Kings presenting gifts to the newborn Christ. In the image the Holy Family stands together on the right side of the image. All three are haloed, with the Christ child sitting on the Virgin's lap, and St. Joseph watching over the Virgin's shoulder.
The first king, a Caucasian man dressed in red with a long white beard kneels at the feet of the virgin and presents the first gift of Gold to Christ. He has removed his crown, which sits on a pillow beside them. A money box sits on the ground between them, open so the gold within is visible.
The Second king bows so that he is below the eye-line of saint Joseph, he hold the incense bowl for frankincense before himself. He is depicted with a short grey beard and he is cloaked in red.
The Third king is a black man with no facial hair and a crown still on his head. He is dressed in red and blue and he presents Myrrh to the Holy Family. The Myrrh is in circular vessel, and he carries a stem of the plant in his other hand.
Above the scene the sky is depicted golden and heaven stand out depicted with a circular symbol in the upper left corner. Rays of light come of fin the direction of the Christ child, depicting his connection to the heavenly realm.

items.title: Santa Croce
items.description:
An oil painting image of the Basilica di Santa Croce (Basilica of the Holy Cross). It is pictured from the front, with it's bell tower on the right side and the plaza stretching out in front of it. The building is the home of the principal Franciscan chapter in Florence.
The Chapel is seen from the Piazza di Santa Croce, with it's Gothic Revival Facade, which was added in the years between 1857 and 1863. The new Facade was designed by Niccolò "Nicola" Matas, a Jewish architect from Acona (6 December 1798 – 11 March 1872). He is responsible for the working of the prominent Star of David at the top of the church and was buried at the threshold to the church, (his tomb was placed there as a means to avoid buying a Jewish man on the catholic consecrated grounds of the church).
The dome of the Pazzi Chapel is visible in the background on the right side. Long shadows are cast over the plaza, which is full of people, indicating the late hour as sun begins to set. The entire scene is bathed in s a soft warm light which reflects off the white facade.

items.title: Greek Icon "Stories of Elijah"
items.description:
A large Icon depicting Scenes from the life of the Prophet Elijah.
Elijah enters the Bible in the Book of Kings by challenging the goddess Baal and her priests, and Ahab, the king of Israel. The challenge comes in the form of a prophecy of a drought, which goes against the powers of Baal, who oversees a domain of rain, thunder, lightning and dew.
The first scene depicted in the panel follows his challenge and a subsequent warning from God to flee Israel. The city can be seen in the distance on the left side of the image. Following God's instructions he seeks shelter by a brook east of the Jordan River. A wide body of water flows down the left side of the panel away from Israel.
Once the brook dries, Elijah follow's god's instructions to proceed to Zarephath in Phoenicia. There, he is put up in the house of and fed by one of the City's Widows. A miracle is performed wherein her flour and oil do not run out and then Elijah raises her son from the dead after he passes away during Elijah's stay. This Scene does not seem to be depicted in the panel.
After 3 years, god foretells the end of the drought and the famine and instructs Elijah to return to Israel and once again challenge Baal and Ahab. His Challenge takes the form of two sacrifices of a bull. One prepared for Baal and another prepared for Yahweh. Both Bulls are prepared and lead to a pyre, and prayers are said for the wood to light. Baal's prophets attempt to light the pyre to no effect, but when Elijah prays a ball of fire falls from the sky ignite his sacrifice. Elijah can be seen praying next to the fire in the lower right of the image. In the Bible the followers of Baal declare for Yahweh and kill the prophets of Baal.
This story ends with Elijah's explosion form Israel by Jezebel, resulting in days spent wandering the wilderness of Beersheba. During this time he travels to Mount Horeb, where Abraham received the 10 commandments. This scene is depicted at the center left of the panel. Elijah wanders, holding his cloak over his head to shield him from the sun as he makes his journey to seek out the lord.
During this Journey, he faces trials of wind, fire and earthquakes and the story continues to take Elijah to a final confrontation with Ahaziah, the son of Ahab. Ahaziah sends three men to try and capture Elijah, but he strikes two of them down with fire called from the sky. When the third man asks for mercy, Elijah agrees to of with him. Ahaziah dies according to a prophecy spoken by Elijah, from injuries sustained in a fall. This scene is again no depicted in the panel.
Elijah's story comes to an end in 2 Kings 2:3-9, where his ascending to heaven is witnessed by Elisha. In the scene a chariot of fire drawn by horses descends to earth, and Elijah is taken away in a whirlwind, leaving behind his mantel for Elisha to catch. This scene is depicted across the upper half of the Panel. Elijah himself rising, haloed and directing the horses, who are the same color as the fiery chariot on which he sits. He is Haloed and looks to the shining rays of Heaven at the top of the panel. Elijah is depicted taking his Mantel at the lower right of the Panel.

items.title: Madonna and Child with Saint John, et al.
items.description:
Oil Painting on Panel. The Madonna sits at the center of the painting with the infant Christ on her lap. To their left (when viewing), a young Saint John (identified throughout the paperwork in Italian as San Giovannino) holds his Cross in his right hand with his arms crossed over his chest in adoration.
Two people stand with the trio, a man on the left side, and a woman on the right. They are identified as Saint Zachariah, the father of John the Baptist, and either Saint Elisabetta or Anna in documentation. As the female saint holds a book, which is an attribute of Anna (Saint Anne in English), this is her more likely identity. Saint Anne is the mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus Christ.
The Iconography in this image is interesting,as the depiction of a sleeping infant Christ on the Virgin Mary's lap is usually reserved for images of the two of them alone, rather than images of them with other people.
A crack runs through the center of the image, thankfully bypassing the important details of each of the figures. Restoration work has been done periodically on the image.

items.title: Portrait of Plato
items.description:
An oil on canvas depicting Plato. Plato is centered in the composition, seemingly emerging from the dark background: he is starkly lit in an otherwise dark composition, his face depicted in chiaroscuro.. His brow is furrorwed and his philosopher's coat (a patchwork tribon) falls off of his right shoulder. He looks intently at the viewer, guesturing towards a mirror with his left hand. The mirror, which he holds with his right hand, is set on a table.
On the table is inscribed: "LA PIV' GRAN VITORIA/ CHE POSSA HAVERE/ VN HVOMO E'VINCERE/ SE' STESSO." This is a passage from Plato's "Laws."

items.title: Madonna and Child with Angels
items.description:
An oil on canvas. The Virgin Mary is centered and takes up almost the whole height of the canvas. A baby Jesus stands on what appears to be a cloud. He is reaching up toward Mary, on arm around her neck and the other placed on her chest. Mary covers his hand with one of her own, while the other is around his waist.
Mary is dressed in her usual: a red tunic with a blue shawl around her shoulders and a gold-detailed veil atop her head. A few blonde curls fall from under her veil. Jesus is dress in his usual as well: nothing! Like his mother, Jesus has a halo above his blonde curls.
Behind the two is a sea of angelic faces, all appearing to be rather young.
This image is attributed to the Master of the Scandicci Lamentation, whose real name and exact life span remains unknown. He was active in Florence in the 16th century.
